blocks.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is an acute, potentially life-threatening metabolic complication of diabetes mellitus caused by significant insulin deficiency, increased counter-regulatory hormones, hyperglycaemia, ketone production and metabolic acidosis.
It occurs most commonly in type 1 diabetes but can also occur in type 2 diabetes, particularly during severe physiological stress or with SGLT2 inhibitor use.

blocks.title: DKA requires urgent hospital treatment involving:

items.text: Identification and treatment of precipitating factors.

blocks.text: Important distinction: Adult and paediatric DKA management protocols are not interchangeable. Children have different fluid, insulin, cerebral injury and monitoring considerations. This chapter treats them separately.

blocks.title: DKA is characterised by three essential abnormalities:

blocks.text: It results from inadequate insulin activity combined with increased concentrations of counter-regulatory hormones, including:

items.text: Insulin deficiency reduces peripheral glucose uptake.
Glucose spills into urine, producing osmotic diuresis.
Free fatty acids reach the liver.

blocks.text: Beta-hydroxybutyrate is the predominant ketone in DKA and is the preferred measurement for diagnosis and monitoring.
Urine ketone testing measures acetoacetate rather than beta-hydroxybutyrate. Therefore, urine ketones may underestimate initial severity and may remain positive during recovery.

rows: Increased hepatic glucose production and reduced peripheral uptake
Increased fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis
Hyperglycaemia-induced water shift and urinary losses

blocks.text: Important prescribing principle: Serum potassium may initially be normal or elevated despite substantial total-body potassium depletion. Insulin treatment can rapidly lower serum potassium.
The 2024 international consensus report uses three components for diagnosing DKA.

rows: Glucose ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L), or previously established diabetes
Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L, or urine ketones ≥2+
Venous pH below 7.3 and/or bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L

blocks.text: All three components must be present.
Important: DKA can occur with glucose below 200 mg/dL, particularly in pregnancy, prolonged fasting and SGLT2 inhibitor use. This is called euglycaemic DKA.
Not every parameter must fall into the same category. Overall severity and clinical condition determine the appropriate treatment location.

A typical normal anion gap is approximately 8–12 mmol/L, depending on the laboratory.
The anion gap is useful diagnostically, but it should not be used as the sole criterion for DKA resolution because hyperchloraemic acidosis may persist after ketones have cleared.

blocks.text: Why?
Glucose often normalises before ketonaemia and acidosis resolve. Stopping insulin simply because glucose has normalised can allow further ketone production.

Critical prescribing safety
Potassium management is one of the most important aspects of DKA treatment.
Total body potassium is depleted in most patients, even when the initial serum potassium concentration is normal or elevated.
Insulin administration, correction of acidosis and fluid replacement cause potassium to move intracellularly and may produce dangerous hypokalaemia.

Separate paediatric protocol
Paediatric DKA requires special attention because children are at risk of cerebral injury during treatment.
The ISPAD paediatric DKA guideline recommends carefully calculated fluid replacement, delayed insulin initiation after starting fluids, and frequent neurological and biochemical monitoring.

items.text: Give IV glucose according to the adult or paediatric emergency protocol.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. Renal and hepatic impairment, pregnancy and breastfeeding

blocks.text: DKA can cause acute kidney injury due to severe dehydration.

items.text: Adjust fluid replacement according to renal function.
Avoid automatic potassium supplementation in anuric patients.
Consider dialysis support in selected patients with severe renal failure, refractory electrolyte abnormalities or fluid overload.

blocks.text: Patients receiving dialysis may not have the usual large fluid deficit. They require individualised fluid and insulin management.
Liver disease may alter glucose production, insulin metabolism and lactate clearance.

items.text: Careful assessment of fluid balance and coagulation abnormalities.

blocks.text: DKA during pregnancy is a maternal and fetal emergency.

items.text: DKA may develop at lower glucose concentrations.
Maternal dehydration and acidosis can compromise fetal wellbeing.
Immediate treatment should not be delayed while awaiting fetal investigations.
Involve endocrinology, obstetrics, anaesthesia and critical care.

blocks.text: Pregnancy-specific DKA protocols should be used. There is no routine role for oral antidiabetic drugs as a replacement for insulin during acute DKA treatment.
DKA itself is not a contraindication to breastfeeding after maternal stabilisation.
Insulin is compatible with breastfeeding.

items.text: Review all other medications for lactation safety.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Monitoring and assessment of treatment response

blocks.text: DKA requires frequent biochemical monitoring.

rows: 2 hours after starting insulin, then every 4 hours
Continuous when indicated by severity or electrolyte abnormalities

blocks.text: Increase monitoring frequency when abnormalities are severe or changing rapidly.
Neurological deterioration requires immediate reassessment.
DKA is considered resolved when:
1. Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate is below 0.6 mmol/L.
AND
2. Venous pH is at least 7.3 OR bicarbonate is at least 18 mmol/L.
Ideally, blood glucose should also be below 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L).
Important: Do not use urine ketones or anion gap alone to determine resolution.
Urinary ketones may remain positive during recovery because beta-hydroxybutyrate is converted into acetoacetate.

Whether the infusion pump is functioning.
Whether infection or another precipitating factor remains untreated.

blocks.text: Essential examination and prescribing points

items.text: DKA is defined by hyperglycaemia or known diabetes, ketonaemia and metabolic acidosis.
Beta-hydroxybutyrate is the preferred ketone measurement.
Total body potassium is depleted even when serum potassium is elevated.
Adult IV insulin commonly starts at 0.1 units/kg/hour.
Add dextrose when glucose falls below 250 mg/dL.
Continue insulin until ketonaemia and acidosis resolve.
Routine phosphate replacement is not recommended.
SGLT2 inhibitors can cause euglycaemic DKA.
Paediatric insulin begins at least one hour after starting fluids.
Never administer a routine IV insulin bolus in paediatric DKA.
Cerebral injury is a major paediatric complication.
Basal insulin must overlap with IV insulin before transition.
DKA can occur in type 2 diabetes as well as type 1 diabetes.

Commonly 20–30 mmol/L of IV fluid when indicated
